extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys/agents, and IPO examiners (India), especially those working on computer-related inventions and pharmaceutical filings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for examination of computer-related inventions (CRI) and selected Section 3 exclusions under the Indian Patents Act (IPO India, CRI Revised Guidelines 2025). Covers technical-character tests, procedural deadlines, opposition/working-statement requirements, and pharma-specific Section 3(d) rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical character
rubrics_metrics.description: Must contribute beyond merely executing on a computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners are directed to identify a 'technical character' that goes beyond software running on generic hardware — i.e., a contribution in the technical domain rather than mere automation of non-technical activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete technical solution
rubrics_metrics.description: Should solve a real-world technical problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examination should focus on whether the invention provides a concrete technical solution using technical means (not an abstract concept). Links to tangible technical advantages or improvements strengthen patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hardware integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Should be tied to specific hardware features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that meaningfully interact with or require particular hardware features are more likely to be treated as technical. Examiners look for specific hardware limitations or implementation details rather than purely abstract or generic computing steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format-agnostic analysis (substance over form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Substance of the invention is assessed regardless of claim/format wording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must evaluate the underlying technical contribution and not be swayed by clever drafting or presenting an abstract idea as a computer-implemented process. The test is one of substance over form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess technical contribution (over claim format)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment should emphasize technical contribution rather than the way claims are drafted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must look beyond the literal format of claims and determine whether there is a genuine technical contribution; claim drafting that disguises an abstract idea should not be sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish CRIs from purely abstract algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should differentiate computer-related inventions from abstract algorithms that lack technical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithms or mathematical methods that do not produce a technical effect or are not tied to a technical implementation should be considered excluded subject matter (see Section 3(k)). Application of the algorithm to solve a concrete technical problem supports patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine whether claims provide 'technical contribution'
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must demonstrably provide a technical contribution to be allowable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of a technical contribution in the claims is a required factor; examiners should identify and articulate that contribution when examining CRIs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3(k) — exclusion of mathematical methods, business methods, computer programs per se, algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical methods, business methods, computer programs per se, and algorithms are non-patentable under Section 3(k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CRI guidelines provide structured tests to determine when such matter is 'per se' excluded versus when it produces a technical effect. Computer programs 'per se' require demonstration of a technical effect/technical contribution to overcome the exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3(d) — new form of known substance not enhancing efficacy
rubrics_metrics.description: A new form of a known substance is not patentable unless it shows enhanced efficacy (Section 3(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly important for pharmaceuticals — polymorphs, salts, esters, combinations, and new formulations of known actives will be refused unless accompanied by data demonstrating enhanced efficacy. Strategic filings should include comparative/experimental data to show an efficacy improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3(b) — inventions contrary to public order or morality
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions contrary to public order or morality are excluded under Section 3(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should refuse or flag inventions that would be inconsistent with public order or morality. No further elaboration provided in the summary, but the exclusion is noted among Section 3 categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3(c) — discovery of scientific principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery of scientific principles is non-patentable under Section 3(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pure discoveries of natural laws or scientific principles are excluded; patentable subject-matter requires application of such principles to a technical purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3(i) — methods of treatment of humans or animals
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods of treatment of humans or animals are excluded under Section 3(i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method-of-treatment claims (medical/surgical/therapeutic methods) are not allowable; applicants should consider alternative claim strategies (e.g., compositions, devices, or diagnostic methods framed to avoid exclusion) where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3(j) — plants and animals (other than microorganisms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plants and animals (other than microorganisms) are excluded under Section 3(j).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims directed to plants and animals are not patentable subject-matter unless they fit exceptions (e.g., microorganisms) recognized by law and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination request timing — 48 months deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: A request for examination must be filed within 48 months of the priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to file the examination request within the 48-month window can result in abandonment or loss of examination rights. Applicants should calendar this deadline early in prosecution planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-grant opposition allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-grant opposition can be filed during examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competitors may file pre-grant oppositions while the application is under examination; applicants should be prepared to respond and consider prosecution strategy anticipating oppositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-grant opposition period — 12 months
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-grant opposition must be filed within 12 months of grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oppositions after grant are time-limited to 12 months; an Opposition Board reviews such oppositions. Applicants and patentees should monitor newly granted patents for potential challenges in this window.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition Board review
rubrics_metrics.description: An Opposition Board reviews pre- and post-grant oppositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Opposition Board process is the designated administrative forum for challenges; strategic considerations include evidence gathering and arguments anticipating Board standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working Statement (Form 27) — annual requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Form 27 (Working Statement) is required to be filed annually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: patentees must file Form 27 reporting the worked status of the patented invention each year; non-compliance can have consequences under Indian practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fast-track examination eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Fast-track examination is available to certain classes of applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eligible categories include Indian applicants, female applicants, government departments, small entities and startups, and eligible international applicants under PPH. Use of fast-track can accelerate prosecution timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case law integration in CRI examination
rubrics_metrics.description: The CRI 2025 Guidelines incorporate 19 case laws to inform examination practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners and practitioners should consider relevant judicial decisions cited in the guidelines for nuanced application of technical contribution and exclusion tests; the case law reflects evolving judicial interpretation of CRIs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured tests for traditionally complex exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2025 guidelines introduce structured tests for algorithms, business methods, mathematical methods, and computer programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidelines aim to provide a systematic approach to evaluate these traditionally difficult areas; practitioners should apply these structured tests when drafting and prosecuting CRI-related claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage for cutting-edge technologies (AI, blockchain, quantum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dedicated guidance and sections address AI/ML/DL, blockchain, and quantum computing within CRI examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidelines explicitly treat emerging technologies with tailored considerations; applicants working in these fields should align claims and specification to show technical contribution in those technical domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic consideration — risk of pre-grant opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-grant opposition can be triggered by competitors during examination, affecting prosecution strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because pre-grant opposition is permitted, applicants should plan prosecution and disclosure carefully (e.g., include supporting data early) and be ready to defend inventive step/technical contribution claims during examination.
